opening_summary: Thirty-four terms for building a game in Godot, from the panels of the editor to scenes, signals, the two clocks and collision. Knowing the exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent precisely what to change.
opening_description: 34 Godot terms: editor, scenes, signals, collision.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often say a scene is the running game. It is not. A scene is a saved tree of nodes, a file. What runs is the scene tree, and it can hold far more. Godot is full of look-alike pairs like that one. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
A scene is
the running game.

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-four terms about building a game in Godot, in four groups. The first group is the editor, with the Scene dock, the Inspector, the 2D, 3D and Script views and the Run buttons. It covers where you look, and what each part is for.

The second group is scenes and nodes. Project, scene, node, script, scene tree, instance, group, autoload, resource, and the export preset and template. These terms say how a game is built and kept together.

The third group is clocks, input and signals. The process function and the physics process function, input action, just-pressed vs held, polling, event-driven and signal. These terms say when code runs, and how the parts of a game talk.

The fourth group is bodies and contact. Area2D, StaticBody2D, RigidBody2D and CharacterBody2D, then collision shape, layer, mask, bitmask and area snapshot. These terms say what can touch what, and what notices it.

This is a drawing of the Godot editor. The Scene dock, lit in red at the top left, shows the nodes of the open scene as a tree. Its Remote tab switches that view to the game while it runs. Here the saved scene has three nodes, and the Remote tab counts seven once mobs have spawned. For example, the Walker platformer's saved main scene looks almost empty, and the Remote tab shows the floor, the spikes and the player that code built.

The FileSystem dock, lit at the lower left, is your view of the project folder. Every file of the game is in it, under the res prefix, written res, colon, slash, slash. The Scene dock shows nodes, and the FileSystem dock shows files. For example, when an AI coding agent adds a new coin scene file to your game, it turns up in the FileSystem dock, and you can open it from there or drag it into a level.

The Inspector, on the right, is where you see and change the properties of whichever node is selected. Here the Player is selected, and its Speed is edited from one hundred sixty to one hundred ninety-two. That is one number, changed in one place. For example, select a moving platform in your level, and the Inspector shows its position and its collision layer, ready to change by hand.

The Node dock shares the right side with the Inspector, on the tab named Node. It tells you which signals the selected node has, where each is connected, and which groups the node belongs to. Here the Player's signal named hit is connected to Main. The Inspector is for properties, and the Node dock is for signals and groups. For example, to check that a coin's body entered signal reaches your score script, select the coin and look in the Node dock.

The same editor drawing, with the top row lit. The 2D, 3D and Script views are tabs that change what the main screen in the middle shows. In the 2D and 3D views you arrange a scene by hand, and in the Script view you write code. For example, you place a platform by dragging it in the 2D view, then switch to the Script view to see the lines an AI coding agent wrote for the player.

Output and Debugger are the panels along the bottom. Output is the running log of whatever the game prints. The Debugger is where an error is reported, with the file and line it came from. Here it reports an error on line twelve of the player script. For example, if your player script prints its speed when it starts, that text lands in Output, and if the script calls a node that does not exist, the error lands in the Debugger.

Project Settings holds values for the whole project, not for one node. The drawing opens it from the Project menu and lists four of them. Sixty physics ticks per second, a name for physics layer four, an autoload, and an input action. For example, the Walker game names its physics layer four Hazard in Project Settings, so you and the agent can call the spikes' layer by name.

The Run and Play buttons sit at the top right. Run Project, also the F5 key, plays the whole game, starting at its main scene. Run Current Scene plays just the scene open in front of you. In the drawing, the first button runs the game with its mobs, and the second runs the player scene alone. For example, to test a new enemy's patrol without playing the whole level, open the enemy scene and press Run Current Scene.

This is a folder listing. A Project in Godot is simply a folder. What makes it a project is a file named project dot godot at the top of it. The res prefix, written res, colon, slash, slash, always means that folder. For example, in the Walker jumpman repository the project is the godot subfolder, so every test run from the command line has to point at that subfolder.

A Scene is a tree of nodes saved to a file so it can be reused, such as a level, a character or a menu. Godot saves it as text, and each line that begins with the word node becomes one node. Here three lines make three nodes, Main, Player and MobTimer. For example, you save a coin as its own scene and place it many times in a level, and an AI coding agent can open that text file and edit it.

A Node is the smallest piece a Godot game is built from. Each node is one object with one job. A Sprite2D draws a picture, a CollisionShape2D holds a shape, and a Timer counts down. A scene is a saved tree of nodes like these. For example, a coin in your game could be built from a sprite node for the picture, a collision shape node for contact, and another node that plays the pickup sound.

A Script is the code that gives a node its behaviour. In this course scripts are written in GDScript. The grey ball has no script and sits still. The red ball's script moves it right at one hundred sixty pixels per second, so after two seconds it has travelled three hundred twenty pixels. For example, the Walker player node carries a script that checks the jump action on every physics tick and sets the velocity.

A small tree of nodes, with columns of numbers. The Scene tree is the whole hierarchy of nodes that exists while the game is running. A scene is the saved file, and the scene tree is what runs. Nodes process from top to bottom, the black numbers. The ready function runs for every child before its parent, the red numbers. For example, a Main script can use its Player and its HUD, the on-screen display, in its ready function, because the children are ready first.

An Instance is a copy made from a saved scene and placed in the running game. The box on the left is the template, the mob scene file. A MobTimer triggers a new instance every half second, until there are four. Then, in this example, the template's radius is edited to forty-five and all four instances change. For example, in a dodge game every creep on screen is an instance of the same mob scene, so an edit to that scene changes every creep.

Now the red instance has its own radius of thirty. That is an override, a change made on one instance. When the template is edited to forty-five, three of the four instances follow it, and the red one keeps its own value. The override wins, for that instance only. For example, you can make a single creep in a level smaller than the rest without touching the mob scene.

This is a row of physics ticks across two seconds. Polling means your code keeps checking, tick after tick, whether something has happened yet. Here Main asks one hundred twenty times whether the player was hit, and only the red tick says yes. For example, the Walker game uses polling for its spikes. On every physics tick a script asks whether the hazard is overlapping the player.

Event-driven means your code waits, and runs only when it is told that something happened. Nobody asks. On the lower line there is one call, at tick seventy-two, the moment of the hit. Polling asked one hundred twenty times for the same news. For example, a pause menu that does nothing until a key press arrives is event-driven, and so is a coin whose pickup code runs only when a body enters it.

A Signal is a node's way of announcing, by name, that something happened to it. Other nodes connect to the signal, and each connection says who listens. The diagram shows five connections into Main, from the Player, the timers and the HUD. No node reaches into another. For example, in a dodge game the Player emits a signal named hit when a creep touches it, and that signal is connected to the game over function in Main.

These are timelines for a slow machine and a fast one, across a quarter of a second. Godot calls the process function each time it draws a frame, so how often it runs depends on the machine. At thirty frames per second it is called seven times. At one hundred forty-four it is called thirty-six times. For example, a coin's spin or a fading menu can go in the process function, because it only has to look smooth.

Godot calls the physics process function on a steady clock, sixty times a second unless you change it. The red marks show it. Both machines get fifteen physics ticks in that quarter second, however many frames they draw. Collision, forces and movement that must repeat exactly belong here. For example, the Walker player runs and jumps inside the physics process function, so a jump plays out the same on every computer.

Now the bars show distance covered in one second. If code adds four pixels on every frame, the slow machine covers one hundred twenty pixels and the fast one five hundred seventy-six. Multiply speed by delta, the time since the last frame, and both cover two hundred forty. For example, an enemy patrol written as a fixed step per frame would walk much faster on a fast laptop.

Keys and buttons on the left all connect to a box named jump. An Input action is a name for something the player wants to do, such as jump, with keys or buttons bound to it. Code asks about the action, never the key. In this example the Space key, the W key and a gamepad button, Pad A, all mean jump. For example, the Walker game binds Space to its jump action, so a gamepad button could be added without touching the player script.

Just-pressed vs held is a choice of button tests. In this example the button is down for thirty ticks. Held is true on all thirty. Just-pressed is true on only one, the tick the press began. For example, test just-pressed for a jump, so holding Space gives a single jump, and test held for running, so the player keeps moving for as long as the key is down.

A ball drops onto a dark floor in this simulated run. The floor is a StaticBody2D. It stays where you put it, whatever hits it, and other bodies collide with it. The ball lands, and the floor has moved zero pixels. For example, the ground and the walls of the Walker level are StaticBody2D nodes. The player stands on them and runs into them, and they never shift.

The red ball is a RigidBody2D. The physics engine is in charge of it. You give it a force or a starting velocity, and the engine works out where it goes. Here gravity pulls the ball down and it bounces five times before it settles. For example, the creeps in a dodge game are RigidBody2D nodes. Each one is given a velocity when it spawns, and the engine carries it across the screen.

The red block is a CharacterBody2D. It goes only where your code sends it. The code sets a velocity, and then move and slide carries the body and keeps it sliding along whatever it hits. Here the block comes down, meets the floor, and runs along it to the wall. For example, the Walker player is a CharacterBody2D, which is why its run speed and its jump are numbers in a script, not forces.

The pink box is an Area2D. It notices when something overlaps it and can emit a signal, but it never stops or pushes anything. The ball passes straight through. The area reports body entered, then body exited, and the ball's speed never changes. A CharacterBody2D blocks, and an Area2D only reports. For example, the spikes and the goal flag in Walker are Area2D nodes. Touching them is noticed, and nothing stops the player.

A Player box faces a column of objects, each marked with a layer. A Collision layer answers the question, where am I. It is the layer, or layers, an object sits in, where others can find it. The editor numbers layers from one, and code uses a value instead. So the Spikes are on layer four, which has the value eight. For example, the Walker game puts its spikes on layer four, named Hazard, and its goal flag on layer five.

A Collision mask is the set of layers an object looks at. It can detect another object only if that object sits in one of those layers. Here the Player scans layers one, four and five, so it detects the Floor, the Spikes and the Goal. The Coin, on layer three in this example, goes unnoticed. For example, if your player never notices a coin it runs through, check whether the player's collision mask includes the coin's layer.

A Bitmask packs many on and off switches into one number, with one bit for each layer. The value for layer n is two to the power of n minus one. So the Player's mask is one plus eight plus sixteen, which is twenty-five, and layer four is the value eight. The red row is the common mistake. For example, an agent that writes collision layer equals four, meaning layer four, has put the object on layer three.

A grey sprite has a red outline inside it. The red outline is the Collision shape, the outline the physics engine tests for contact. The sprite is only the picture the player sees. In this made-up example the art grows to one hundred twenty-eight pixels wide and the shape stays at fifty-four. For example, when Walker's player art was swapped for a wide mascot, the collision shape stayed small, so an arm can seem to touch a spike with no contact at all.

An Area snapshot means an area's list of overlaps is refreshed only once in each physics step, so it can be a tick old. The top row is the truth. The player stops touching at tick four. The middle row is the list, and on that tick it still says touching, the red cell. For example, Walker once counted a second death right after a respawn, because the list still held the spikes. The fix discards two ticks after a reset.

Red and dark dots sit under a single line of code. A Group is a label you can put on any number of nodes, so that one call acts on all of them. In this made-up example the five red nodes are in a group named mobs. One call group line frees all five, and the three dark nodes are untouched. For example, when a dodge game restarts, it clears every creep off the screen with that one call.

An Autoload is a script or scene that Godot loads at the start and keeps when the game changes scene. Here a menu and then the levels run in turn. Each scene's own variable starts over, while the autoload's score keeps adding up, to twelve in this example. For example, a global script that carries the score from level to level, or one that handles every change of scene, is an autoload.

A Resource is a bundle of data with a declared type that several nodes can share. You write your own by extending the Resource class. Change the tuning resource's speed once to one hundred ninety-two, and the Player and the HUD both get it, while the Test keeps its typed-in one hundred sixty. Unlike an autoload, a resource is data, not a node. For example, Walker's tuning resource holds the run speed, and one of its tests carries its own copy of that number.

An Export preset is the saved set of choices for building the game for one platform, which files to include, where the output goes, and the options. An export template is the ready-made engine for that platform, without the editor, that your project's data is packed into. Preset, template and project combine into the exported game. For example, to ship your platformer for the Web you write a Web preset, and the export still fails until the templates for your exact engine version are installed.

Each pair sets look-alike terms side by side. A Scene is a saved tree of nodes, in a file. The Scene tree is the running tree while the game plays. In Walker the saved main scene holds one node, and the running game holds at least thirteen.

The process function runs once per frame, and its rate varies. On the left, seven calls with uneven gaps. The physics process function runs at a fixed rate, sixty a second. On the right, fifteen calls with equal gaps.

A Collision layer says where an object is. It labels the Player as layer two. A Collision mask says what an object scans for. Here the Player scans layers one, four and five. The layer is where I am, and the mask is what I notice.

The Collision shape is what physics uses. In this drawing the red capsule stays fifty-four pixels wide. The Sprite is what the player sees. The grey art scales up to one hundred twenty-eight pixels wide, and the shape does not follow. New art never changes the contact by itself.

A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it, beside a chart of what it does. Make the player touch the coin becomes, put the coin on layer two, and add two to the player's collision mask, so one becomes three. Mask one, no contact. Mask three, yes.

Make movement the same on every computer becomes, move in the physics process function, sixty ticks a second on any machine. The process function ran seven times on one machine and thirty-six on the other. The physics process function ran fifteen times on both.

Jump when I press space becomes, bind Space to the input action named jump, and test just-pressed on each tick. For a press of half a second, held is true on thirty ticks, so thirty jumps. Just-pressed is true on one.

Tell the main scene when the player dies becomes, the Player emits a signal named hit, connect it to the game over function in Main, and do not poll. Over two seconds, polling asks one hundred twenty questions. The signal makes one call.
Show me what the game really contains becomes, run it, switch the Scene dock to its Remote tab, and count. The saved main scene file holds one node. The running game holds thirteen, at least.

This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a change to a Godot game. First, check that the saved scene matches the running tree. Run the game and look at the Remote tab of the Scene dock.
Second, check that movement which must repeat exactly runs in the physics process function, on the fixed tick. In the process function it would differ from machine to machine.
Third, check that the input is an action in the Input Map, not a raw key. Then decide whether you want just-pressed, true for one tick, or held, true for as long as the button is down.
Fourth, ask who emits and who connects. If code asks the same question on every tick, consider whether a signal should replace the polling.
Fifth, check that the collision layer and mask use the bitmask value, two to the power of n minus one, and not the layer number. Then check that the collision shape still matches the art.
Sixth, ask whether the area's overlap list could be a tick old, and whether the shared number sits in one resource. Then say it exactly. Not make it collide, but layer two, mask three.

recap_lines: Each editor dock has one job, and the Remote tab shows the running game.
A scene is a saved file, and the scene tree is what runs.
A signal tells you once, where polling asks on every tick.
The physics process function runs at a fixed rate on every machine.
A collision layer says where an object is, and a mask says what it scans.
The collision shape is what physics uses, not the sprite you see.

your_turn.command: Quiz me on Godot terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use the terms scene, scene tree, instance, signal, polling, input action, just-pressed, collision layer, collision mask and collision shape. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 5 (The scene tree and instances), step 2: the caption ends on '4 of 6 instances follow the template (radius 45).' but only four instances are drawn. In renderTree the count vis = Math.floor(t / 0.6 * 4) is never clamped to 4, so it reaches 6 by the end of the step. It should say '4 of 4'. The narration says four.

Slide 14 step 1 and the last line of slide 15 put the coin on layer 2 ('Put the coin on layer 2 (value 2)', 'layer 2, mask 3'). Slide 10 puts the Player on layer 2 and the Coin on layer 3 (value 4), and Chapter 4 names layer 2 'Player'. By slide 10's own picture the exact instruction would be 'coin on layer 3 (value 4); add 4 to the player's mask'. Slide 14 also starts the player's mask at 1 where slide 10 gives it 25.

Two different example games share the file name main.tscn and are never told apart. Slides 2 to 4 show main.tscn with 3 nodes (Main, Player, MobTimer, the Dodge the Creeps shape) and 7 nodes in the Remote tab. Slides 13 and 14 say 'main.tscn: 1 node' and 13 running nodes (walker-jumpman). The Inspector on slide 2 also shows Player Layer 1, Mask 1 while slide 10 says the Player is on layer 2 with mask 25. A viewer can take these as contradictions. The narration names Walker on slide 13.
Slide 1 says '34 terms from Chapters 1 and 4, the glossary and the Godot editor', but export preset and template come from Chapter 15 (slide 12 cites it).
Slide 14 step 1: the 'yes' label is clipped. It is white text right-aligned at x=580 on a red bar that ends at x=574, so its last letter falls off the bar onto white.
Slide 10 steps 1 and 2: the Player's own layer ('layer 2 · value 2') is printed at the top left of the picture, far from the Player box, so it looks like a heading and not the Player's label.

Slide 12 step 4: the caption says of preset and template 'Both must match your engine.' Chapter 15 only says templates are kept by exact engine version; a preset is a recipe for one platform. The same caption runs into the TELL THESE APART box below it, and the step sits under the badge 'Illustrative data' though it shows no data.

Slide 3 step 4: with player.tscn open in the main screen, the Scene dock still lists Main, Player and MobTimer, the nodes of main.tscn. Slide 3 step 1: the Script view shows 'extends Area2D' (a player script) under the file label main.tscn.
Slide 9 step 2: the counter stops at 'tick 239 of 240'.
Slide 11 step 1 and slide 13 pair 4: 'sprite 128 px wide' at 'scale 0.80' implies art 160 px wide, which is never shown, and the caption says 'Swap the art' while the picture scales it.

Wording differs between the course glossary and the slides: the glossary defines Polling as asking 'every frame' and Just-pressed as true 'on the frame a button went down'; slides 6 and 8 say 'every tick' and 'the tick'. Term names also vary inside the deck: the map says 'Run buttons', 'layer' and 'mask' where the slides say 'Run and Play buttons', 'Collision layer' and 'Collision mask'.
